name: Clobetasol for hair

card.summary: A super-potent prescription topical steroid that dermatologists use on alopecia areata patches to try to bring back hair.
card.note: Prescription-only; strong topical steroids can thin skin and, with heavy use, suppress the adrenal axis.

quick.overview:
Clobetasol propionate is a very high-potency topical corticosteroid, sold as creams, ointments, foams, lotions and scalp solutions. For hair, doctors prescribe it for alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss, by calming the immune attack on the follicles.
The appearance payoff is regrowth in bald patches on the scalp, beard or eyebrows. Wikipedia notes that topical steroids often do not reach the hair bulbs deeply enough and have had limited success in severe cases, while small patches often regrow by themselves.
quick.how: It is prescribed and applied to affected patches under a doctor's directions, often as a foam or solution for the scalp. It is sometimes used alongside injected corticosteroids, minoxidil or newer treatments, and any regrowth takes weeks to months.
quick.risks: Side effects include skin irritation, redness, acne-like bumps, visible small blood vessels and, with prolonged use, skin thinning and stretch marks. Systemic effects such as adrenal suppression have been reported. It is prescription-only in the US; safety in pregnancy is unclear.

lead: Clobetasol propionate is a 'super-high potency' topical corticosteroid, the top of the seven-class US scale. Its listed uses include eczema, psoriasis and lichen sclerosus, as well as autoimmune conditions such as alopecia areata [1].

In hair care it is used to try to regrow hair lost to alopecia areata. Patches are treated with the cream, foam or solution so the steroid suppresses local inflammation around follicles. Wikipedia's alopecia areata article states that none of the existing treatments is curative or preventive, that spontaneous remission makes judging treatments difficult, and that clobetasol or fluocinonide has had limited success in severe cases [2].
The drug appears on forums mostly in other contexts. On T Nation, one user in 2011 asked about its effect on testosterone after a doctor prescribed it for a forearm patch of hair loss [3].

chain: Suppresses immune attack on follicles in a patch
Hair may regrow in the patch
angle.text: A dermatologist may prescribe it to bring back hair in alopecia areata patches. It does not address pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia), which has different causes.

infobox: Rx-only in the US; some countries differ

paras: For hair, the use is alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition. Topical steroids are one of several options, alongside injected triamcinolone, minoxidil, anthralin and, more recently, JAK inhibitors such as baricitinib, ritlecitinib and deuruxolitinib [2].

Wikipedia reports that creams are less effective and slower than injections, and that topical steroids often do not penetrate deeply enough to reach the hair bulbs [2]. It cites a 2020 systematic review in which over 50 percent regrowth occurred in 80.9 percent of patients given injected triamcinolone, a different route from clobetasol cream [2].

Common effects include irritation, dryness, redness, pimples and dilated small vessels; serious effects include allergic reactions, cellulitis, adrenal suppression and Cushing's syndrome [1]. Misuse as a skin-whitening cream has been linked to thin, easily bruised skin and permanent stretch marks [1].
It is sold under many brand names and as a generic; it entered medical use in 1978 [1]. In the US it requires a prescription [1].
No studies have tested clobetasol for hair specifically; treatment evidence for alopecia areata is summarised in review articles [2].
